Correct, latency is not critical.

Yes, it can get expensive. We do something in financial markets where the cost of a single end to end task could be $100. That doesn't mean cost doesn't matter though, it matters a lot - if we screw up and it propagates, it's money down the toilet. And if we could get the task down to $20, it would make a difference.

Interesting. Seems to me like latency is not critical in your application and you are doing something more like background processing rather than serving humans on the other side in real time.

Also, some of what you describe sounds expensive. Do you find these techniques + cheaper models better than single-shot with larger models?

There are all manner of documented architectures in papers and books, I don't know that there is anything new under the sun at this point, the devil is always in the details. That said, some of the things we use off the top of my head: generate multiple responses using different models and have a third model judge the best answer; generate an answer and have another model critique the answer and then a third take the answer and critique and generate a new answer; multi-model debate; iterate in a loop either x times or until some condition is satisfied; pipelines of specific single calls to check for specific conditions.

I'd say in general, with respect to errors/low quality responses etc you have to be extremely clear about what you are doing because once you get into the weeds, what is and is not an error is very grey in many cases.
Thanks for the response! Curious, can you expand on the architecture, how does that work? If you can share of course.

To answer your question - we use cheaper models to just flag if something looks obviously flawed. That covers the vast majority of things because it's the propagation of obviously stupid stuff that causes a problem for our system. To the extent we are doing something sophisticated, we use an appropriate architecture, like it's built into the system.

children.text:
Good questions.

Agent observability is based on similar primitives as regular observability (OTEL), but is wildly different. Trace payloads are huge, and errors are much more subtle, they are not increased latency or elevated 500 response rate. We recommend tracing everything in detail, and reading a few traces manually at the beginning while you iterate. At scale, the answer is almost always use another LLM look at your traces, which is what this post is all about.

Evals are critical. I really recommend adopting the Anthropic's capability / regression eval model [1]. We also deeply believe that agent evals should be end-to-end, and as high-level as possible. This again often involves a quality LLM-as-a-judge, tuned on a set of manually labelled data.

With this idea in mind (to answer your question), we think that, for eval datasets, the most crucial bit is to be able to store input of what your agent was asked about in production. Collect a certain distribution of inputs for happy and unhappy cases, and then run evals on those inputs. That's why Laminar went great lengths to help our users automatically get actual inputs their users send to their agents [2].

[1] https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for...

[2] https://laminar.sh/blog/extracting-tasks-from-agent-runs

How do you reuse traces as benchmarks (eval datasets)? Is it about being able to synthesise an agent session from the trace, and having another agent watch the first agent's behavior? Having trouble wrapping my mind around all the little details.

Yes, significantly - even when adding in vendor costs etc. In general though it is best at answering routine questions or ones a customer could get by reading the docs. The net result then is the ones left for the humans are the harder ones.

We’ve also heard from other companies that as the first line paper cut questions get answered, customer adoption increases - which further increases the “hard” support questions.

Lesson learned for me on that one that was rolling out a support agent led to both a better experience for our customers and an increased need for talented human engineers.
hm, did the cost of tickets processed by an agent go down tho?

We ran into an interesting side effect of agent performance that we needed to explain in our results to our executive team. In our case we were rolling out an AI support agent that could help resolve customer problems. At the start we had calculated the total time and human cost per support ticket going back a few years. After a few months of running the AI agent, we found that both our time and cost per ticket had increased - but then digging in, the issue was that our overall cost and time had decreased and it was just that the more complicated issues the agent wasn't able to answer were the ones now going to the humans, skewing our per ticket cost up.

So in this case it's not that it was a different failure, it was that a signal that seemed to indicate failure was actually a signal of success.

text:
Hi HN, we’re Robert and Din from Laminar (https://laminar.sh). We’ve been building open-source observability for AI agents since 2024. Recently, we released flow-1, a model trained with RL to find errors in agent traces. On our benchmark (https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1), it matches GPT-6-sol in detection quality while being 23x cheaper. This makes it affordable to analyze every production agent trace, without sampling.

Here’s a one-minute walkthrough: https://youtu.be/KJa3h6ZJNLQ

We also put together a post with example traces and analyses from flow-1 and other models: https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1-in-action

Agent observability is crowded, so instead of a bullet list of how Laminar differs from X, we’ll explain how we’re solving agent observability from first principles.

Agents now run for many steps and fail implicitly. An agent can click the wrong button or cite the wrong document while every call completes successfully. These errors are the most useful ones to catch and understand. To find them, you need to understand what the agent was trying to do and inspect its LLM calls and tool results. Simply looking at the final agent output is not enough.

Collecting traces alone doesn’t solve this. A lot of agent observability platforms are still data collectors at their core. You can end up paying to store traces that nobody has time to read or extract value from.

Using another LLM to inspect traces is THE solution, but capable models are expensive at scale and cheaper ones often miss errors or flag unrelated things.

So we built our model to solve exactly this problem. We finetuned a small OSS model and then post trained it with RL on thousands of synthetic investigations of realistic agent workflows in software, legal, customer support, etc. We got a model that is both good at agent trace analysis and very cheap to run.

flow-1 runs inside a harness we call Signals. It acts as a coding agent, treating an agent trace like a repo, with each span (an LLM call, tool call, etc.) as a file. It starts from a compressed string representation of a full agent trace and a user prompt, then greps across spans and reads the relevant ones in full.

The beauty of Signals is that it can respond to a general prompt. You can ask it to identify user frustration, check whether your browser agent completed a checkout, and so on. It’s not limited to raw error detection. It returns findings as JSON in a schema users can freely define. We call these signal events.

Once you’re analyzing every trace, you also have too many individual events to read. That’s why we automatically group similar signal events into clusters. You can see recurring problems and how often they happen, then drill into individual events and the traces behind them.

You can use traces from a cluster to build an eval dataset for that type of failure. You can then use your favourite coding agent to hillclimb on those evals and check that the fix works across these cases before shipping it to prod.

Trace → analyze → catch errors and form clusters → fix → release. Making this loop easy is why we built Laminar.

We’ve put the same thought into the rest of Laminar. Our blog (https://laminar.sh/blog) explains how looking closely at how agents actually work led us to build 20x trace compression, a custom SQL query engine and automatic task extraction.

Laminar is Apache 2.0 and self-hostable (https://github.com/lmnr-ai/lmnr). We make money from the managed cloud.

We’d love to hear how you track your agents’ performance today. How much do you learn from user feedback versus your own monitoring? And when you fix something, how do you check that it hasn’t introduced a different failure?
